text: In August nineteen seventy-three, Johan Cruyff boarded a plane in Amsterdam bound for Barcelona.
At that moment, Barça had not won the Spanish league for thirteen years.
Nine months later, they were champions — and they had done it by humiliating Real Madrid five–nil at the Bernabéu. This is the season that changed Barcelona.
This is the story of nineteen seventy-three, seventy-four: one player, one season, and a club that rediscovered itself.
Part one. A club in the shadows.
In the late sixties and early seventies, Barcelona were a big club living in Real Madrid's shadow. Madrid had the European Cups, the league titles, and the reputation.

For many Barça supporters, the club also meant something beyond football. Spain was still ruled by Franco, and Catalan identity was pushed to the margins. The stadium was one of the few places where people felt free to express it.
What Barça lacked was a team to match that feeling.
Then, in nineteen seventy-three, Spanish football opened its doors to foreign players again, after years of restrictions.
Barça already had a Dutch coach: Rinus Michels, the man who had built Ajax's great team and invented much of what people called Total Football.
And Michels's greatest player at Ajax was ready to leave Amsterdam. He had just won his third European Cup in a row. He was the best footballer in Europe.
Part two. The transfer.
The deal made Cruyff the most expensive player in the world at the time.
Real Madrid had been interested too. But Cruyff chose Barcelona — and later explained that he could never play for a club associated with the dictatorship.
There was one problem. Because of registration delays, he couldn't play official matches straight away. He had to watch as the season began without him.
And without him, Barça struggled. They started the season badly, and by the autumn they were near the bottom of the table.
Expectations had been sky-high. Now people were starting to wonder if one Dutchman could really change everything.
Part three. The debut.
In late October, Cruyff was finally registered. In his first official league match at the Camp Nou, against Granada, he scored twice.
From that day, the season turned around. A team that had been losing started to win — and kept winning.
Cruyff didn't just score. He organised everyone around him, pointing, shouting, moving teammates into position. He was the coach on the pitch.
He also argued — with referees, with opponents, with his own teammates. Cruyff never stopped talking on a football pitch.
To some people it was arrogance. To his teammates, it was leadership. He was telling them, all game long, exactly where they needed to be.
Part four. The impossible goal.
In December, against Atlético Madrid, Cruyff scored a goal people still talk about.

A cross came in high, towards the far post — and seemed to be going behind him. Cruyff leapt into the air and, with his body almost horizontal, flicked the ball into the net with the outside of his heel.
In Spain, it's remembered as the impossible goal. Photographs of it became some of the most famous images of his career.
Part five. The nought–five.
And then came the night that defined the season. On the seventeenth of February, nineteen seventy-four, Barça went to the Bernabéu.
They scored once. Twice.
Three, four, five. Real Madrid nil, Barcelona five, at Real Madrid's own stadium. Cruyff scored one and was involved in almost everything.
For Barça supporters, it was more than a football result. In Catalonia, people remember celebrating in the streets as if something much bigger had been won.
Barça had won at the Bernabéu before. But never like this — and never with a team that seemed to be playing a different, more modern kind of football than its great rival.
That same month, his son was born. Cruyff reportedly named him Jordi — after Catalonia's patron saint, Sant Jordi — at a time when Catalan names were officially discouraged.
Part six. Champions.
By the end of nineteen seventy-three, Cruyff had won the Ballon d'Or for the second time.
By February, Barça had beaten Madrid five–nil in their own stadium.
And in the spring, Barcelona were champions of Spain — the first league title in fourteen years.
That summer, Cruyff went to the World Cup with the Netherlands, reached the final, and was named the best player in the tournament. Barça added another Dutch star, Johan Neeskens.
Many expected a dynasty. It didn't happen. Barça wouldn't win the league again for more than a decade. But the season had planted something that would grow later.
Part seven. The seed.
Cruyff's playing years at Barça ended in nineteen seventy-eight. But he had fallen in love with the city, and the city with him.
Ten years later, he came back as coach — and built the Dream Team, La Masia's philosophy, and the style that still defines Barça today.

Without nineteen seventy-three, seventy-four, there's no reason to think he'd ever have come back. The season didn't start a dynasty. It started a relationship — and that turned out to be worth much more.
Which was the biggest Barça win over Madrid ever — the nought–five of seventy-four, the two–six, or the five–nil of twenty ten? Tell me in the comments.
